caption:
Stiff neck after your morning laps? Your breathing might be part of the story.

In freestyle, much of the turn to breathe should come from rolling the torso. When the body stays flat, the neck does more of the turning, and lifting your head for air adds extra twist. Over a full session, that adds up.

What tends to help: roll your body to breathe, keep one goggle in the water, mix in breaths to both sides, and loosen your mid-back on land first.

Arm tingling or weakness, building headaches or dizziness are worth an assessment. Our chiropractors at Hybrid Physio combine hands-on care with exercises for the pool. Book online via the link in bio.

Should you stretch after a massage? Gently, yes.

Many people feel looser for a few hours after a remedial massage. That's a handy window for an easy walk or the home exercises you've been given. If an area felt tender during treatment, keep it light for the rest of the day rather than stretching hard.

caption:
Living with scoliosis and wondering whether Pilates is a good fit? Here's what to expect.

Scoliosis is a sideways curve of the spine, often with some rotation, and it varies a lot between people. Many live active, comfortable lives with it.

Clinical Pilates isn't about straightening the spine. Goals usually centre on strength, control, comfort and confidence in movement. A program starts with an assessment of how you move and breathe, then mixes some side-specific work with plenty of training for both sides.

A curve that seems to be changing, or numbness or weakness in the legs, is worth discussing with your GP or specialist. Our Pilates team at Hybrid Physio tailors each program to you. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Waking up with a stiff neck? Sleeping face down could be part of it.

Lying on your stomach means turning your head fully to one side to breathe, and holding that end position for hours can leave some people stiff. A thick pillow adds more twist. If you wake up fine, there's no need to change a thing.

If you're stiff most mornings, try a thin pillow or none under your face, and ease towards side sleeping by hugging a long pillow with one under your top knee.

caption:
Calf cramp mid-run again? It's not always about salt.

Dehydration and electrolytes often get the blame, but research suggests muscle fatigue plays a big role. Cramps tend to hit late in a session, or when you go harder or longer than usual.

On the spot, stop and gently lengthen the muscle: pull your toes towards you and hold. Most cramps ease within a minute or two. If the same muscle keeps cramping, strengthening it with calf raises two or three times a week can help it cope. Build distance gradually.

See your GP if cramps happen often at rest, or come with calf swelling, redness or warmth. Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios can help with the training side. Book online via the link in bio.

Japan ski trip booked? A few weeks of prep can make day three feel a lot better.

Skiing and snowboarding keep you in a bent-knee position for long runs, with twists and sudden loads. After a Sydney summer, most legs aren't used to that, so thighs tire and knees work harder.

caption:
Four months after ACL surgery and the knee feels fine. So why not play this weekend?

A new graft keeps remodelling for many months, and the knee can feel good well before it's ready for cutting, jumping and contact. Rehab usually builds strength first, then running, then jumping and landing, then change of direction.

Rather than a calendar date, return decisions often use strength and hop tests compared with the other leg, plus confidence in the knee. Research suggests returning to pivoting sport too early is linked with a higher chance of reinjury.

Side planks load the muscles along the side of your trunk and hip together. That can help with carrying on one side, changing direction and balancing on one leg.

Start on your knees with your elbow under your shoulder. Hold 10 to 20 seconds, 3 times each side, breathing normally. When that feels easy, straighten your legs. Add time before difficulty, and keep holds clean rather than long.

caption:

Jumping and landing put some of the biggest loads through your knees in sport, especially in netball, basketball, volleyball and touch. When ankles, knees and hips bend together, that load is shared.

Hybi's drill: jump off a low step with both feet, land soft and quiet with knees in line with toes, and hold 2 seconds. Do 10 reps, then progress to single-leg hops and direction changes. Squats, lunges and step-downs build the strength behind it.
